title: Transpilation basics
description: Transpilation converts source code from one language to another at the same abstraction level — TypeScript to JavaScript, Python to... well, usually not Python. Unlike compilation to machine code, the output is meant to be read and maintained. The translator parses the source AST, maps constructs to target idioms, and emits target source. Fidelity is measured by running the original test suite against the translated code.
mechanism: Parse source -> AST -> transform (construct mapping table) -> emit target. Mapping table covers expressions, control flow, and standard library calls. Untranslatable constructs are flagged, not silently approximated.
algo: O(n) AST transform. Correctness from the mapping table's coverage, verified by the test suite.

title: Semantic equivalence
description: A translation is correct when the translated program behaves like the original on all inputs — semantic equivalence, not textual similarity. In practice this is checked by differential testing: run both versions on generated inputs and compare outputs. Full equivalence is undecidable in general, so translators aim for test-equivalence plus review of the tricky constructs (concurrency, exceptions, numeric edge cases).
mechanism: Generate inputs (property-based); run source and target; compare outputs and side effects. Divergence = bug in the mapping table. Equivalent modulo known differences (float formatting) is the practical bar.
algo: O(test cases * runtime). Coverage of the input generator bounds confidence.
demo:
# differential test: original Python vs 'translated' JS-like logic, same inputs
def py_total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

def js_total(xs):  # the translation under test
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s = s + x
    return s

import random
random.seed(1)
diverged = 0
for _ in range(500):
    xs = [random.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))]
    if py_total(xs) != js_total(xs):
        diverged += 1
        print('DIVERGENCE on', xs)
print('500 random inputs, divergences:', diverged, '(differential testing = equivalence check)')

title: AST transforms
description: AST-to-AST transformation is the clean architecture for translation: parse once, apply a pipeline of tree rewrites, emit. Each pass does one thing — desugar comprehensions, map builtins, adjust scoping — and the pipeline composes. Debugging is sane because you can dump the tree between passes. String-level translation (regexes on source) is the alternative everyone regrets.
mechanism: Passes: parse -> normalize (desugar) -> map constructs -> map stdlib -> emit. Each pass is a NodeTransformer; passes run in fixed order; untranslatable nodes raise with location.
algo: O(passes * nodes). Pass isolation makes each transform testable alone.

title: Idiom mapping
description: Languages have idioms — the natural way to say things — and good translation maps idiom to idiom, not construct to construct. Python's list comprehension becomes JavaScript's .map(); Go's err-check becomes Rust's ?. A construct-level translation produces code that works but reads like a tourist; idiom mapping produces code natives would write. The mapping table is the translator's real intellectual property.
mechanism: Idiom table: (source pattern, target idiom, conditions). Match patterns on the AST (not text); prefer idioms when the pattern matches exactly, fall back to literal translation otherwise. Document every mapping with examples.
algo: Pattern match O(patterns) per node; table-driven, so adding languages is data, not code.
demo:
# idiom table: source pattern -> target idiom (not construct-to-construct)
IDIOMS = [
    ('[f(x) for x in xs]', 'xs.map(x => f(x))', 'py->js listcomp'),
    ('{k: v for k, v in items}', 'Object.fromEntries(items)', 'py->js dictcomp'),
    ('x if c else y', 'c ? x : y', 'py->js ternary'),
]
print('%-28s -> %-28s (%s)' % ('source idiom', 'target idiom', 'direction'))
for s, t, d in IDIOMS:
    print('%-28s -> %-28s (%s)' % (s, t, d))
print('construct-level translation reads like a tourist; idiom mapping reads native')

title: API mapping
description: Standard libraries differ — Python's os.path.join vs Node's path.join vs Rust's Path::join — and translation must map API calls, not just syntax. API mapping tables record (source API, target API, argument adaptation): some map 1:1, some need argument reordering, some have no equivalent and need a shim. Coverage of the mapping table decides whether the translated program even imports.
mechanism: Table: source fully-qualified name -> (target name, arg transform). Shim library implements unmapped APIs in the target language. Report unmapped calls as errors with the closest candidates.
algo: O(calls) table lookup. Shim coverage is the long tail — automate its generation from docs where possible.

title: Type mapping across languages
description: Types do not translate 1:1: Python's int is arbitrary precision, JavaScript's number is float64, Rust's i32 is 32-bit. The mapping must preserve semantics or document the change — silent int->float64 conversion breaks code that relies on big integers. Nullable types, generics, and error types need explicit policies. This is where translations fail quietly.
mechanism: Type table with semantic notes: (source type -> target type, precision/behavior notes). Emit warnings for lossy mappings (bigint -> number). Map error idioms: exceptions -> Result/Option, None -> null/undefined/nil per target.
algo: O(types) table-driven. Lossy mappings warned, never silent.
demo:
# type mapping with lossiness warnings (never silent)
TYPES = {
    'int': ('number', 'LOSSES precision > 2^53: use bigint'),
    'str': ('string', 'ok'),
    'list': ('Array', 'ok'),
    'None': ('null | undefined', 'check both in JS'),
}

for src, (tgt, note) in TYPES.items():
    flag = 'WARN' if 'LOSS' in note or 'check' in note else 'ok  '
    print('[%s] py %-6s -> js %-14s %s' % (flag, src, tgt, note))
print('silent int->float64 breaks big-int code: warn, never silently convert')

title: Error handling translation
description: Error idioms are per-language: Python raises, Go returns (value, err), Rust returns Result, Erlang crashes and supervises. Translating error handling means translating the idiom — a Python try/except becomes Go's if err != nil at every call, or Rust's ? operator. Getting this wrong produces code that compiles but drops errors silently, the worst kind of translation bug.
mechanism: Map: exceptions -> (return err / Result / throw per target). Insert checks at every fallible call; map exception types to error values. Verify: the translated tests must exercise every error path the original tests did.
algo: O(fallible calls) transform. Error-path test coverage is the verification.

title: Concurrency model translation
description: Concurrency is the hardest translation target: threads vs async/await vs goroutines vs actors have different semantics for shared state, cancellation, and ordering. A threads-and-locks program translated to async/await naively will deadlock or race differently. The safe approach maps concurrency patterns (worker pool, pipeline, fan-out) to target-native equivalents rather than translating primitives.
mechanism: Pattern table: thread pool -> async semaphore pool / goroutine pool; locks -> channels/mutex per target; thread-locals -> context vars. Verify with stress tests and race detectors, not just unit tests.
algo: Pattern-level mapping; verification by stress + race detector. Primitive-level translation is unsound.
demo:
import asyncio

# pattern: worker pool. Threads version (source) -> async version (target).
async def worker(q, results):
    while True:
        item = await q.get()
        if item is None:
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.001)  # the work
        results.append(item * 2)
        q.task_done()

async def main():
    q, results = asyncio.Queue(), []
    workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(q, results)) for _ in range(4)]
    for i in range(10):
        q.put_nowait(i)
    await q.join()
    for _ in workers:
        q.put_nowait(None)
    await asyncio.gather(*workers)
    return sorted(results)

print('async worker pool result:', asyncio.run(main()))
print('pattern mapped (pool->pool), not primitives (thread->task): semantics preserved')

title: Test-driven translation
description: The test suite is the translation's specification: translate the tests first, run them against the translated code, and let failures drive the mapping table. Tests-as-spec catches semantic drift that code review misses — a mistranslated edge case fails loudly instead of shipping quietly. Coverage of the translated tests should match the original's; gaps are untranslated behavior.
mechanism: Translate test files (same AST pipeline); run both suites; diff results. Failing translated tests pinpoint mapping bugs. Mutation-test the translation: if a mutant survives in one language but not the other, the suites differ in strength.
algo: O(tests) per run. The suite is the executable spec — keep it in sync.
demo:
# tests are the spec: translate them first, let failures drive the mapping
def total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

# translated test suite (same assertions, target language idioms)
tests = [
    ('empty', [], 0),
    ('single', [5], 5),
    ('negatives', [-1, -2, 3], 0),
    ('floats', [0.1, 0.2], 0.30000000000000004),  # float edge: same in both
]
failed = [name for name, xs, want in tests if total(xs) != want]
print('translated suite: %d/%d pass' % (len(tests) - len(failed), len(tests)))
print('failures:', failed or 'none -- mapping table is correct for these cases')

title: Incremental migration
description: Big-bang rewrites fail; incremental migration ships: the strangler-fig pattern runs old and new side by side, routing traffic gradually. For language translation this means FFI boundaries — call the translated modules from the original program (or vice versa) — and expanding the translated surface over releases. Each increment is independently testable and rollback is flipping the router.
mechanism: FFI/interop layer at the boundary; feature flags route traffic; expand module by module; delete the original when coverage hits 100%. Monitor both sides' metrics during the transition.
algo: O(modules) increments. Each increment independently shippable — risk bounded per release.
demo:
# strangler fig: route gradually from old to new implementation
old_calls, new_calls = [0], [0]

def old_total(xs):
    old_calls[0] += 1
    return sum(xs)

def new_total(xs):  # translated version, proven by tests
    new_calls[0] += 1
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

TRAFFIC = 0.5  # flag: 50% to the new implementation
import random
random.seed(7)
for _ in range(1000):
    xs = [random.randint(0, 9)]
    got = (new_total if random.random() < TRAFFIC else old_total)(xs)
    assert got == sum(xs)
print('traffic split 50/50: old=%d new=%d, all results correct' % (old_calls[0], new_calls[0]))
print('raise the flag gradually; rollback = flip it back')

title: LLM-assisted translation
description: LLMs translate code fluently but unreliably — they hallucinate APIs and drop edge cases. The working pattern is LLM-draft plus deterministic verification: the model proposes the translation, the AST pipeline checks construct coverage, and the translated test suite proves equivalence. Humans review the diff, not the blank page. Translation quality jumped, but the verification pipeline is what makes it shippable.
mechanism: LLM translates file-by-file with the mapping table as context; deterministic pass verifies every construct was mapped (no silent drops); test suite runs; human reviews the diff. Unverifiable constructs fall back to manual translation.
algo: LLM O(tokens); verification O(nodes + tests). The pipeline, not the model, guarantees quality.
demo:
# LLM draft + deterministic verification: the pipeline that makes it shippable
import ast

source = 'def total(xs):\n    return sum(xs)\n'
# 'LLM draft' (simulated): a plausible translation
draft_js = 'function total(xs) { return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }'

# deterministic verification: every source construct mapped?
needed = {type(n).__name__ for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(source))}
covered = {'FunctionDef', 'Return', 'Call', 'Name', 'Module', 'Load', 'arguments', 'arg', 'Expr'}
missing = {n for n in needed if n not in covered and not n.startswith('_')}
print('draft:', draft_js)
print('constructs needing mapping:', sorted(needed - {'Load', 'Store', 'Module'}))
print('unmapped constructs:', missing or 'none -- draft passes verification')
print('then: translated test suite runs; human reviews the diff')

title: Verifying translations
description: Translation verification stacks three techniques: the translated test suite (behavioral), differential testing on generated inputs (broad), and manual review of untranslatable constructs (targeted). Formal equivalence proofs exist only for tiny languages; in practice, the combination catches what matters. The residual risk lives in concurrency, floating point, and platform APIs — review those by hand, always.
mechanism: Suite -> differential fuzz -> targeted review of flagged constructs. Track verification coverage: which constructs were proven by tests vs reviewed by humans. Ship only when both lists are empty of unknowns.
algo: O(tests + fuzz cases + flagged constructs). No single technique suffices; the stack does.

title: Standard library mapping
description: Standard libraries are the long tail of translation: every language's stdlib has hundreds of modules with subtly different semantics. Mapping tables cover the common 80 (strings, collections, math, I/O); the rest get shims implemented in the target language or explicit 'not supported' errors. Automated doc-mining generates candidate mappings; humans curate the semantic notes.
mechanism: Mine API docs for signatures; align by name + signature similarity; human curates semantics. Shims: implement source semantics in target (e.g., Python's pathlib in JS). Version the table with both languages' releases.
algo: O(apis) mining; curation is human. Coverage measured as % of calls in the corpus mapped.
demo:
# stdlib mapping coverage: measure what fraction of real calls are mapped
MAPPED = {'len', 'str.upper', 'list.append', 'os.path.join', 'json.dumps', 're.match'}
corpus_calls = ['len', 'str.upper', 'os.path.join', 'os.fork', 'json.dumps',
                're.match', 'socket.bind', 'list.append']
mapped = [c for c in corpus_calls if c in MAPPED]
print('mapped %d/%d calls (%.0f%%)' % (len(mapped), len(corpus_calls), 100 * len(mapped) / len(corpus_calls)))
print('unmapped:', [c for c in corpus_calls if c not in MAPPED], '-> shims or errors')
print('the common 80 map cleanly; the tail is shims + curation')

title: Human review of translations
description: Automated translation still ends with human review — but review of a diff, not a blank page. Reviewers check the flagged constructs (untranslatable, lossy, concurrency), the semantic notes on API mappings, and the test results. The review checklist is generated from the translation's own uncertainty: every warning the pipeline emitted becomes a review item. No warnings, no review needed — the pipeline earned the trust.
mechanism: Pipeline emits warnings with locations and reasons; review tool presents them as a checklist with the diff context; sign-off records which items were accepted. Metrics: warnings per KLOC trends down as the mapping table improves.
algo: O(warnings) review. The pipeline's job is minimizing warnings without hiding real issues.
demo:
# the pipeline's warnings become the review checklist
warnings = [
    ('types.py:12', 'lossy int->number mapping (precision > 2^53)'),
    ('net.py:88', 'concurrency primitive mapped: manual stress-test required'),
    ('util.py:3', 'unmapped API os.fork: shim written, review it'),
]
print('REVIEW CHECKLIST (auto-generated from translation warnings):')
for loc, why in warnings:
    print('  [ ] %-12s %s' % (loc, why))
print('no warnings -> no review needed: the pipeline earned the trust')

title: Translation benchmarks
description: Translation quality is measured, not asserted: benchmarks run translators over corpora of real programs and score compile rate, test pass rate, and human-judged idiomaticity. The corpus must cover the hard parts — concurrency, metaprogramming, FFI — not just algorithms. A translator scoring 99% on sorting algorithms and 40% on real web services is a demo, not a tool.
mechanism: Corpus of (source, tests) pairs across domains; metrics: % compiling, % tests passing, idiomaticity rating. Ablate: which mapping-table entries drive the failures. Publish per-domain scores, not just aggregates.
algo: O(corpus * translate + tests). Per-domain breakdowns prevent aggregate-gaming.
